Insider interpretation as the starting point of scholarly description, without adjudicating truth

claims.claim: Religious experiences can be characterized generally as experiences that seem to the person having them to be of some objective reality and to have religious import.

Religious experience is distinguished from religious feeling: a feeling that occurs in a religious context does not count as a religious experience unless it seems to the person to be an experience of a religiously significant reality.
"Religious experience" was not widely used as a technical term before William James's The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902), after which it became a standard scholarly phrase.

In The Varieties of Religious Experience, William James identified four marks of mystical experience: ineffable (defying adequate verbal description), noetic (carrying a sense of insight or knowledge), transient (not sustainable for long), and passive (the subject feels the will is in abeyance, as if grasped by a superior power).

Rudolf Otto, a German theologian and historian of religions, used "numinous" (from Latin numen, "spirit") for the felt presence of the holy and described it as a mysterium tremendum et fascinans — a mystery before which humanity both trembles and is fascinated; Otto held the numinous could not be derived from anything other than an a priori sacred reality.

Mystical experience involves deliberately undertaken practice aimed at realization, unity with the divine, or direct experience of ultimate reality, whereas many religious experiences (such as those attributed to figures like Paul) come unsought.

Sociologists distinguish the experience, beliefs, and rituals of a religion, and describe religious experience as the conviction or sensation of being connected to the divine, often felt when people pray or meditate.

Scholars study religious experience through first-person accounts and phenomenological description of the basic structures of consciousness; naturalistically oriented psychologists such as Freud and Leuba explained religious experience as a projection of wishes and desires, a claim others rejected.

Neurological explanations of religious experience are contested: similarities between brain states during meditation and during certain seizures, mental disorders, or drug states are cited as reasons to doubt the experiences, but every experience is accompanied by a corresponding brain state, so that fact alone does not establish illusion.

Philosophers of religion debate whether religious experience can justify religious belief: defenders such as Swinburne and Alston argue it can, while critics argue differences from sensory experience undermine its evidential value; this lesson references the debate only, as philosophy of religion owns it.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does James's criterion of ineffability define all mystical experience?
positions: James held that ineffability is essential to mystical experience.
Later scholars (e.g., Alston) used "mystical" more broadly, and the SEP notes James's criterion would rule out many cases commonly understood as mystical.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes the four marks to James, notes that his criterion was contested, and treats mystical experience as one type among several rather than the whole category.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Are neurological similarities between religious experience and seizures, disorders, or drug states evidence that religious experiences are illusory?
positions: Some researchers treat the similarities as reasons to deny the veridicality of religious experiences.

Others (e.g., d'Aquili and Newberg) study the neurological basis without inferring illusion, and critics (e.g., Ellwood) note that every experience has a corresponding brain state, so the similarity alone cannot show illusion.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents neuroscience as a contested research area and does not take sides.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Can religious experience justify religious belief?
positions: Defenders (Swinburne's Principle of Credulity, Alston's perceptual account, Plantinga) argue experience can provide grounds for belief.
Critics argue religious experience differs from sensory experience in ways that undermine its evidential value.
James held that mystical experiences are authoritative for the person who has them but cannot give grounds to others.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the debate neutrally, attributes it to philosophers of religion, and references the philosophy-of-religion topic as the owner of the question.

sourceRecords.title: The Varieties of Religious Experience: A Study in Human Nature (1902)
sourceRecords.notes: Read the Gutenberg plain-text transcription (ebook 621) on 2026-08-21. Verified in the Mysticism lectures James's four marks of mystical experience — ineffability (defies adequate verbal expression), noetic quality (states of insight), transiency (cannot be sustained for long), passivity (will in abeyance, grasped by a superior power) — and in the Conversion lectures the account of conversion as a gradual or sudden process by which a divided self becomes unified. 1902 work in the U.S. public domain.
